title: Word Search
statement: You get a grid of letters and a word. Decide whether the word can be spelled by a path of cells where each step moves up, down, left or right to a neighbour. A single cell may not be used twice in the same path.

example.caption: CATS is spelled along the top row, then down from the T to the S.

idea.sentence: From each start cell, match one letter at a time. Mark the cell as in use while exploring from it, and restore it when you back up, so other paths can use it.

jargon.plain: Make a choice, explore everything that follows, then undo the choice and try the next one.
Depth-first search: follow one path as far as it goes before trying another.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: a grid of one-letter strings, then the word. Keep the grid to 2 by 3.

compare.bruteLabel: Copy the visited set at every step
compare.unit: cells touched (rough, exponential in the word length)

rows.name: Copy the visited set
rows.note: Pass a fresh set of used cells down each step. Same paths, but every step copies up to L cells.

rows.name: Mark in place and restore
rows.note: From each start, a path has at most 3 new neighbours per step (not the one it came from) and is at most L deep. Space is only the recursion.

fast.takeaway: Both are exponential in the word length. Writing # into the board and putting the letter back keeps each step cheap and needs no extra set.

stages.title: Pick a start
stages.note: Try each cell as the first letter. Stop with true at the first success, false if none works.

stages.title: Match or stop
stages.note: If every letter is matched, the word is found. If the cell is off the board, already in use, or the wrong letter, this branch is a dead end.

stages.title: Mark and explore
stages.note: Write # into the cell so the path cannot revisit it, then try right, down, left and up for the next letter.

stages.title: Restore
stages.note: Put the original letter back. This is the undo: other paths, and other start cells, see the board as it was.

edges.title: One-cell board
edges.why: The start cell matches the only letter, and k reaches the word length at once.

edges.title: Word longer than the board
edges.why: The second A would need a different cell. The only neighbour is off the board, and the first A is in use.

edges.title: Reuse is not allowed
edges.why: The second C is the cell the path started on. It holds # at that moment, so it does not match.

edges.title: First start fails
edges.why: Starting at the top-left B fails. The next start, the A, works. Starts do not stop the search on a miss.

gotchas.text: The board is changed while searching. Restore every cell before returning, on the success path too, or the caller's board stays full of #.
Chain the four calls with ||. It stops at the first true, so later neighbours are not explored. Do not store them in an array first, which would run all four.
Convert the board to [][]byte once. board[r][c] != word[k] then compares two bytes, with no string allocation. Remember a string cell holds one letter, so cell[0] is the byte.
dfs calls itself, so declare it first with var dfs func(...), then assign it. A short := declaration cannot refer to itself.
Check the bounds before indexing the board, and keep the word-length check first. Doing it in the other order reads past the end or fails a finished match.

recap.key: From each cell, match letter k. Put # in the cell, try four neighbours with k + 1, then put the letter back.
recap.complexity: Time O(m·n · 3ᴸ). Space O(L) for the recursion.
moves: Try every cell as the start
Stop on a full match, or on a wrong, used or off-board cell
Mark the cell, then try the four neighbours with ||
